n: Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt for Refractory Ascites

faq.a: Diuretics fail in refractory ascites because portal pressure remains high; TIPS directly lowers that pressure.
faq.q: Why not just increase diuretics instead of TIPS?

faq.a: In low‑resource settings, ultrasound‑guided puncture can substitute, but success rates are lower.
faq.q: Can TIPS be done without fluoroscopy?

faq.a: Hepatic encephalopathy due to bypass of hepatic detoxification.
faq.q: What is the main long‑term risk after TIPS?

exam: During a bedside exam you note shifting dullness and asterixis after a recent TIPS – what does this indicate and how would you manage? — Identify hepatic encephalopathy, start lactulose, assess shunt patency.

A patient with refractory ascites is HIV‑positive and on antiretrovirals; why must you be cautious with TIPS? — Discuss drug‑induced hepatotoxicity, potential for worsening encephalopathy, and need for CD4/viral load assessment.

Explain why right‑heart failure is a contraindication for TIPS and how you would screen for it without echocardiography. — Describe clinical signs (jugular venous distension, peripheral edema) and bedside ultrasound of IVC.
You have no access to HVPG measurement; how do you decide whether TIPS will benefit the patient? — Use clinical portal hypertension signs (splenomegaly, varices) and refractory ascites criteria.

After TIPS the patient develops a sudden rise in serum bilirubin to 6 mg/dL – what are possible causes and immediate actions? — Consider shunt thrombosis, hepatic ischemia; obtain Doppler, give albumin, consider shunt revision.

Compare TIPS with repeated large‑volume paracentesis in terms of survival, quality of life, and resource use in a low‑income hospital. — Highlight fewer procedures, better QoL with TIPS, but higher upfront cost and need for expertise.
What prophylactic measures reduce post‑TIPS encephalopathy and why? — Use lactulose, avoid excessive protein restriction, monitor ammonia; explain gut flora modulation.
ai.title: Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt for Refractory Ascites
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: TIPS creates a channel between the portal and hepatic veins to lower portal pressure, offering symptom relief in refractory ascites when medical therapy fails. It is especially relevant in low‑resource settings where liver transplantation is unavailable.

b: Indicated after ≥4 weeks of optimal diuretic therapy with persistent grade 2–3 ascites
Contraindicated in severe hepatic encephalopathy, uncontrolled infection, or right‑heart failure
sections.p: Refractory ascites is fluid accumulation that persists despite sodium restriction and high‑dose diuretics. TIPS reduces portal hypertension by diverting blood flow, decreasing transudation into the peritoneal cavity.

t.b: Is there portal vein patency? – Confirms suitability for TIPS; if unavailable, rely on clinical signs of portal hypertension
Baseline liver function and renal reserve – High bilirubin (>5 mg/dL) predicts poor outcome; if labs unavailable, use clinical jaundice and encephalopathy grade

b: HVPG >12 mmHg is the threshold for clinically significant portal hypertension
Target post‑TIPS HVPG is ≤12 mmHg or a reduction of ≥20 % from baseline
sections.p: Portal hypertension drives ascites formation; TIPS lowers the hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) to <12 mmHg, which usually halts fluid accumulation.

t.b: What is the pressure gradient? – Gradient >12 mmHg confirms need for shunt; post‑procedure <12 mmHg predicts response
Risk of encephalopathy? – Rising levels after TIPS suggest need for prophylactic lactulose

b: Improves quality of life by reducing paracentesis frequency
May precipitate hepatic encephalopathy; monitor mental status closely
sections.p: In East African hospitals, hepatitis B, schistosomiasis, and alcohol dominate cirrhosis aetiology. TIPS offers a bridge to transplant or palliation where transplant is not feasible.

t.b: Is encephalopathy present? – New confusion after TIPS warrants lactulose or rifaximin
Is ascites decreasing? – >2 kg loss or 2 cm girth reduction within 1 week indicates success

b: Always state you must optimise diuretics and sodium restriction before TIPS
Mention that TIPS is contraindicated in severe encephalopathy (West Haven grade III–IV)
sections.p: Examiners often test decision‑making, complications, and interpretation of limited investigations.

t.a: Scenario: patient with refractory ascites and creatinine 1.8 mg/dL
t.b: Is TIPS safe? – Borderline renal function; assess for hepatorenal syndrome; consider albumin infusion before procedure
What next? – Start lactulose; evaluate shunt patency with Doppler if available

b: Assuming any ascites is refractory without confirming diuretic resistance
Neglecting to screen for right‑heart failure, which worsens after shunt
sections.p: Errors arise from overlooking contraindications, misreading pressure gradients, and failing to anticipate encephalopathy.

whenToSeekHelp: New onset haematemesis or melena suggesting variceal bleed
Rapid abdominal distension with hypotension indicating shunt thrombosis
